One of the most fun spellcasting systems I have ever seen! Knowing what to cast in what situation has never been more satisfying. The concept itself of combining elements to make spells had me sold, and the game itself managed to value that potential. 

The freedom of doing whatever the fuck you want whenever you want is amazing. No bullshit mana bars. No crappy skill trees. No cooldowns. Pure, unaltered, raw power, scaled with your skill level. Some DBZ style shit here.

There are downsides though:
- arrowhead did one of the crappiest netcodes in existence. Crashes happen. Connections don't. Hosting doesn't work most of the time. Multiplayer is such an amazing experience, be it Adventure, Challenge or Versus and crap like this stands in the way. If you can overlook that, this game is easily a 88/100, but with the crappy 1998 multiplayer, the score is rightfully dragged down to 74.
- latency in this game is on steroids for some reasons, probably bad optimization
- too few people play, and because of the crappy matchmaking system you need to know people's numbers and have friends that play
- they pump out a ton of DLCs, something that I hate on principle
- the devs aren't really fixing much. They're adding more stuff and grabbing lodsemoneh
- limited to a max of 4 players per game (and I think having way more would've been so much fun; game is not made for this)

The PROS:
- the combinations you can do with those 8 elements is mindblowing
- so much fun in all 3 modes: Adventure, Challenge and especially Versus if you are at a high skill level and monsters are too weak
- skill level can be INSANE. One guy can take out 100 other wizards and 1000 mobs, without getting a scratch.
- single player is a lot of fun: comedic story, fun missions, DLCs aren't bad, they're just short
- various robes you can put on, with various abilities
- at high levels of play, the PVP aspect is balanced, but at low-med levels, you can spam a few spells and always win since people don't know how to counter them
- Versus mode is LODSA fun at high skill levels
- huge skill roof
- great physics and offense-defense mechanics
- intuitive effects of your spells

I recommend it a lot, especially if it's on sale. About the DLCs? I'm not sure. Having the base game is enough imo, the DLCs are really worth it for the extra robes that you can have fun with.

[h1]REVIEW[/h1]
[b]Magicka[/b] is a very enjoyable game. Fun, funny, and challenging... it makes for a very amusing experience. The standard campaign is relatively brief, but there is a lot of DLC content. Some of it is cosmetic and can be ignored, but much of it provides actual content and you will likely want to pick it up to get the full experience. [b]Magicka[/b] also makes for unique and enjoyable multiplayer gameplay, if you find some people to play with. 

As I alluded to, the innovation inherent in the main gameplay mechanics is the primary reason that [b]Magicka[/b] is something worthy of being in your library. There isn’t much else quite like it, and absolutely nothing of the same caliber.  You have to rapidly press certain button combinations to cast various spells while simultaneously controlling your character and aiming in an isometric view. It is pretty unique and intense. I personally found it more comfortable with a controller, but it also works well with a standard keyboard and mouse set up.

And while the exciting gameplay is definitely the soul of the game, it is also quite funny and charming too. The art style is very fitting to the mood of the game; and although the graphics aren’t the best, they feel appropriate. With the addition of the mumble language, silly plot, and hyperbole of blood/gore, the jovial nature of [b]Magicka[/b] becomes clear. This lighthearted atmosphere synergizes well with the unique gameplay to create an experience that is incontestably fun.

The key feature of the game being the innovative gameplay mechanics, I recommend anyone looking for some variety check it out if they haven’t already. I highly recommend playing with other people though; it’s much more fun and much less frustrating (since you can revive each other).

Also the [i]Versus[/i] and [i]Survival[/i] modes are pretty fun, especially since the game supports local-coop (as in sitting on a couch with your friends, as it was in the old days).

Magicka is one of my favorite games, and one of the few that does a good job making you feel like a wizard.


The Good:

The crown jewel of Magicka's design is its spell creation system.  It was not the first video game to allow you to design spells by selecting the path, area of effect, effects, and intensities.  The Elder Scrolls: Arena had that in 1994, and there may be earlier examples I don't know about.  It may be the first to allow you to create spells on the fly.  It is also noteworthy for having no limits based on a mana pool or cooldowns.  Instead, the main balancing forces are enemy resistances and the destructive power of your own spells.  It's very easy to make a mistake and kill yourself or your allies.

Magicka is also well known and loved for its voice acting.  Everyone speaks a mix of broken Swedish and jibberish.  Vlad is an over the top Romanian vampire in denial.  Death and Fafnir also sound great.  I would love to know what sort of processing they performed on their voices.

Magicka has one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard.  It's bombastic, complex, and memorable.  Unfortunately it may be hard to appreciate with it often being drowned out by the sounds of the chaos around you.


The Bad:

Magicka is very buggy, even by modern PC gaming standards.  Crashes and hangs are common.  Weapons and staves, which may be unique, frequently clip through the map and disappear into the void forever.  Players lose connection in online games often.  The DLC is even worse.  [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/73058/]The Stars Are Left[/url] has an unpatched bug on the last level, where if you don't pass through the doors in the order the developers expected you to, not only does it crash, but it corrupts your save so you have to start that DLC over.  The fact that is still unpatched is shameful, by the way.

Difficulty does not scale based on the number of players.  The main game isn't that difficult to get through solo, but some of the DLC is very hard without a full party.  I found the final fights in [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/73115/]Dungeons and Daemons[/url] and [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/73058/]The Stars Are Left[/url] to be impossible to solo.

The 76 metascore is the result of what Magicka was when it came out: A hidden gem executed okey-ishly and with some bugs. But that's way too far from the game Magicka is today...

The gameplay is a bit hard to explain as there are truly no games like Magicka: Top down isometric spell casting & mixing shmup with always-on friendly fire is the shortest way to put it. The long one is: You see your wizard from a top-down-with-an-angle perspective, you can cast 8 elements: Fire, Life, Electricity, Water, Cold, Earth, Arcana/Death, and "shield" which gives any combination of elements a defensive use of sorts. All this elements are on their own very weak but once you combine them you can get deadly creative. From mini-volcanoes that light enemies on fire and explode when touched to steam-compressed mines that send foes (and friends) flying away Team Rocket-style to Death-electric beams that freeze to freaking Meteor Showers to casting Death Itself (whom kills someone on-screen at random).

Now remember that the game has always-on friendly fire. Yup, it's a madhouse.

If Mario Party destroys friendships, Magicka will obliterate blood-related family ties. But in the nicest, funniest and best ways.

As a lover of couch co-oping, well-executed games, friendship, and... well, games in general, I urge you, TRY MAGICKA. It's very unlikely you'lle ever regret it.

I'm genuinely shocked by the state of this game. It was released 7 years ago, and it's had loads of DLC & even a sequel. Yet it's plagued by bugs and poor design choices. I was really looking forward to it. The humor is right up my alley - equal parts cheesy, referential, full of puns. The art design is nice. I was expecting to endure the combat mechanics, but...I actually love them. They're brilliant - hard to describe, simple to learn, quick to develop, and unlike anything else I've ever played.

And it's all ruined because level after level is plagued by bugs. In three straight levels, I experienced:

1. A bug that made the camera leap to a completely different part of the level, even as combat was still going on. The camera kept trying to re-center, but failed, zooming out and re-locating itself at the far corner of the map.

2. A bug that saw my character repeatedly fall through the world - not in a scripted or intended way, but through the gameworld itself.

3. When the camera restricts to a certain part of the level for a boss fight (intended, so you can't run away or kite enemies), but then traps you behind a corner of level architecture where you can't fight the enemies.

None of these bugs would be major issues, but if you die, you have to restart the level from the beginning or a checkpoint. Sometimes this just means replaying a minute or two, but sometimes it means replaying 5-10 minutes each time. By this point, I'd say well more than half of my deaths have been due to bugs. The combats themselves are enjoyable, and I don't mind dying when combat is hard. But if you die once honestly and two more times because of bugs, you can spend 20 minutes playing a 5 minute level. That gets old fast.

It's a shame. The humor is exceptional, combat itself is well-balanced, and the gameplay reaches surprising depths based on simple concepts. But it's just a buggy mess. I'd like to enjoy it, but it won't let me. I'm amazed they were able to pump out so much DLC before fixing the core game.

Magicka is certainly a flawed game that has its charm. The main gimmick here is being able to combine elemental spells to be able to attack in different ways which made the first few hours of just messing around really fun; that was until the frustration set in.

Many enemies in this game will just one shot you. I love playing difficult games normally, but this doesn't mesh well with the unique combat system of experimenting with different spell combinations. The best way to handle any combat situation was one of two things: spam lightning bolts on outdoor levels, or try to get enemies wet so you can freeze them and throw a rock at them. At some points the best option was to just rush past a section entirely. Despite the game giving so many options, I quickly felt limited with how I could approach combat.

I think that Magicka definitely had the potential to be a really good game, but the last few hours I felt I was playing out of obligation to see it out. The game's comedy was fine at first but also felt worn out by the end, especially with half of the humor being references that by now are incredibly dated. I don't blame them as much as this was 2011, but still.

It's something I only lightly recommend against as there is a genuine game underneath all these problems that had a lot of effort put into it, but it's ultimately a relic of the past that didn't age as well as it could have. There are still people that are passionate about the game many years later for a reason, I wish that the game still kept getting updates for their sake.

Magicka is the only video game in existence that will truly let the player harness his own magic in real time. The spellcasting system is amazingly well designed. The characters are cool, the soundtrack is both immersive and epic, the humor is good and filled with innuendos and easter eggs/references. I would never have thought that such a casual game would have so much quality to it.

The community is incredible. Mods. Fan content. Insanely high-level PvP. Custom Challenges and even modded adventures... There are guides to help learn about spellcasting skills, speedrunning, downgrading to earlier versions and help prevent crashes so that the unstability of the game is not an issue anymore.

It's no wonder people keep coming back to that game from time to time even after more than a decade. It's that good. The kind of game you will always return to for some quick silly and action-packed epic fun in solo or multiplayer every now and then because you will always keep it in your heart.

If the developers would have patched it and showed it additional attention, I'd give it a 10/10. Unless you can overlook the shoddy execution, it's distinctly possible you will regret purchasing Magicka. I'd steer clear unless you aren't bothered by that sort of thing.

Lots of games punish you hard for being a wizard. At the start of the game, you get your one or two spells, and then you have to pretend you're a fighter or run away useless.

This is not one of those games. In this game, you actually feel like a wizard. The only consequences for letting off as many of your most overpowered spells as you can is that maybe one of your friends gets caught in the blast. But you're a mother effing wizard, so resurrect the poor sucker and keep going.

There is a story, but the game doesn't really expect you to pay attention to it. You're a murder hobo on a quest to save the world by killing whatever happens to be in your way. But that's not the point of the game.

The point of the game is the magic system. It's by far the most unique way of handling magic I've ever seen. It takes a bit of getting used to, but once you get the hang of it it is supremely satisfying to let of a huge string of different spells in quick succession, subtlety tweaking your spells to suit the situation.

Or you could just spam QFASA over and over, if that's your thing.

Final note: the game is really designed to be played in co-op. You can play single player, but you're missing out on the full experience.

Magicka is a comical indie action-adventure game where you play as an unassuming wizard attempting to save the world from evil. That might sound cliche though its intentional and the game is full of jokes and satire. You have 8 different elements to choose from and you can combine them into powerful spells with devastating effects. You will need to think fast on your feet as to which spells are best for the given situation thus you will need to use strategy as some levels are quite challenging. The graphics and effects on the spells are done well for an older indie game and the gore setting is a nice compliment. The controls are fine, though the aiming might take a little getting used to and the magic combinations will require some memory. The story is short but charming with some funny "twist and turns". The dialogue is well written, and I found myself chuckling at the game quite often. The level design is good with lots of enemies to wreak havoc on and blast to oblivion. There are a lot of cool and unique wizards with varying abilities to choose from. There is also a nice selection of game modes aside to the story which are all fun to play. Magicka is catered to coop play, and you can play up to 4 players. It will be hard not to laugh, maybe even cry, while playing this game with a friend. However there are some parts of the game that are extremely buggy and some content is almost impossible to complete in the games current state due to crashing errors which caused a fair amount of headache. I was able to download a previous version of the game off of https://steamdb.info/app/42910/ to complete the game though it still crashed here and there. If you can overlook the bugs and crashes Magicka is wickedly fun and a classic indie game well worth a try!

Magicka is a rather unique action-adventure game set in a high fantasy world, loosely based on Norse mythology, with satire, humor, and references to pop culture and other games sprinkled throughout.

The spell system is the star of the show here, as it should be. You play as [strike]Invoker[/strike] a mage with access to eight basic elements (water, life, shield, cold, lightning, arcane, earth and fire) that can be combined in different ways to create different spells. 

Since this is an action-adventure, and not an RPG, there are no classes, no leveling, and most importantly no mana bar to limit your spell casting. Plus you'll have access to the majority of spells right from the beginning of the game.

This spell system is very fun to use, encouraging experimentation and rewarding dexterity, adaptability, and creativity.
